Errors returned by typed read, write and read_ranges expose .kind and .retry_safe. The kind is one of not_found, already_exists, conflict, gap, permission_denied, unavailable, timeout, corrupt, invalid, cancelled, unknown_outcome, or the compatibility categories not_a_directory, is_a_directory, io, not_supported and other. Standard Python exceptions remain available: FileNotFoundError, FileExistsError, PermissionError, TimeoutError, ValueError and NotImplementedError. Additional OSError subclasses are ConflictError, GapError, UnavailableError, CorruptError, CancelledError and UnknownOutcomeError. GapError is available for backends with positioned writes; byte writes do not produce it themselves. Argument errors raised before backend dispatch do not necessarily have operation metadata. retry_safe=True means repeating the operation is safe. False includes cases where safety cannot be established. Transient S3 read failures are safe to retry; an uncertain write is not. Legacy file-handle operations retain their existing error contract.

S3 typed writes send one PUT attempt. Following an uncertain response to write(..., condition=Missing()), the backend reads the object and compares its SHA-256 checksum with the supplied bytes. Matching content acknowledges success; different content returns ConflictError. An absent object or failed verification returns UnknownOutcomeError with retry_safe=False. Local exclusive writes use the same content check after an I/O failure. An ETag is never treated as a content checksum. Recovered success acknowledges matching content for immutable publication; it does not establish ownership of a lock or prove which writer created the object. A definitive precondition failure remains a conflict, including when existing content matches. Ordinary overwrites and Match writes with uncertain outcomes return UnknownOutcomeError without content-based recovery.

Native Python handles and the filesystem wrappers publish buffered writes on explicit close() or clean context-manager exit. discard() closes the handle without publishing pending data. Exceptional exits and finalizers discard. Uncompressed text handles returned by fs.open follow the same rules. Direct local append writes are immediately visible and cannot be rolled back. Explicit flushes can pass text to the underlying handle. External wrappers, including compression and fsspec.open’s OpenFile, control their own close behavior; their exception handling is outside this lifecycle contract. S3 exclusive handles still buffer the complete object. Ordinary S3 writers use multipart uploads for large objects; abandoned uploads are aborted on a best-effort basis. A process crash can leave multipart uploads requiring the store’s retention policy.

s: Default methods keep native backends small
x: The Rust FileSystem trait follows fsspec’s template-method pattern. A backend implements primitive operations such as listing files, reading metadata, opening files, copying, and removing files. t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
x: A Rust crate compiled into a Python extension is private to that extension. When fsspec-rs, fsspec-db, and fsspec-kafka each compile fsspec_rs in, a process loads three copies of its code and three registries, so a backend registered by one extension is invisible to the others. Rust has no stable ABI, so a dyn FileSystem cannot be passed from one extension to another either. libfsspec fixes both with a C ABI. The registry, its instance cache, and the built-in backends are compiled into that one shared library, and every extension links it dynamically. A filesystem is passed between extensions as an opaque handle with a table of C function pointers, which every compiler and language supports. The work is split across three crates so that only one of them has shared state: fsspec_rs has the traits and backends. Compiling the traits into several extensions is harmless; its own registry stays private to the binary that compiles it in. fsspec_capi builds libfsspec and is the only crate with the shared registry. fsspec_sys declares the C functions without implementing them. Extensions depend on it to reach libfsspec; it must never depend on fsspec_capi, or every extension would export it

Supported modes are rb, wb, ab, and xb, plus the aliases r, w, a, and x at the Rust layer. Python wrappers expose binary file objects that implement read, write, seek, tell, flush, close, readable, writable, and seekable. with fs.open("/tmp/fsspec-rs/out.bin", "wb") as f: f.write(b"payload") with fs.open("/tmp/fsspec-rs/out.bin", "rb") as f: f.seek(2) print(f.read()) auto_mkdir=True creates missing parent directories for write, append, exclusive-create, and copy operations. With the default auto_mkdir=False, the operating system reports an error if a parent directory is missing. wb and xb files are buffered in memory and written when the file is closed. The contents go to a temporary file next to the target, which is synced and then renamed over the target, so other readers see either the previous contents or the complete new contents. flush() does not make partial contents visible. xb fails at close if another writer created the file after it was opened. ab files append to the target directly.

Local filesystem methods delegated to Rust include: Listing and metadata: ls, info, exists, isdir, isfile, size Reads and writes: open, cat_file, pipe_file, head, tail, read_text, write_text, touch Directory operations: mkdir, makedirs, rmdir, walk, find, du Mutation and transfer: rm_file, rm, cp_file, copy, mv, get_file, put_file The cache_type, block_size, and max_blocks options are accepted by open() for API compatibility but do not change local read behavior. Local reads use direct filesystem operations.

MemoryFileSystem wraps the Rust MemoryFs backend, which keeps files in process memory. Every instance shares one store, so a file written through one MemoryFileSystem is visible through all of them until the process exits. import fsspec from fsspec_rs import MemoryFileSystem fs = MemoryFileSystem() fs.pipe_file("/data/example.txt", b"hello") with fsspec.open("memory-rs://data/example.txt", "rb") as f: print(f.read()) Paths are rooted at /. Writing a file needs no mkdir: directories exist while a file below them does, as in fsspec’s MemoryFileSystem. mkdir creates an empty directory that persists until rmdir or rm. Written files become visible when they are closed, so readers never see partial contents. The store is separate from fsspec’s Python memory://. In Rust, and to C, C++, and other extensions through libfsspec, the same store is memory://.

S3FileSystem wraps the Rust S3Fs backend, which uses Apache Arrow’s object_store crate and runs its async S3 calls through an embedded Tokio runtime. The Python protocol is s3-rs, so it can coexist with s3fs. from fsspec_rs import S3FileSystem fs = S3FileSystem(bucket="my-bucket", region="us-east-1") fs.pipe_file("reports/hello.txt", b"hello") print(fs.cat_file("reports/hello.txt"))

S3FileSystem is constructed for one bucket. Method calls can use keys within that bucket: fs.ls("reports") fs.info("reports/hello.txt") fsspec URLs include the bucket. _get_kwargs_from_urls() extracts constructor options from the URL: with fsspec.open( "s3-rs://my-bucket/reports/hello.txt", "rb", region="us-east-1", ) as f: print(f.read()) Object names are stored internally without a leading slash. Directory entries are S3 prefixes, not real directories; mkdir() and rmdir() are no-ops.

Credential resolution follows this order: Explicit constructor arguments: key, secret, token, region, endpoint_url, and anon fsspec.config.conf["s3"], including values populated from fsspec config environment variables object_store’s own AWS credential chain, such as environment variables, profiles, and instance or task roles client_kwargs={"endpoint_url": ...} is accepted for compatibility with s3fs. The Rust backend allows plain HTTP when the endpoint starts with http://, as used by local S3-compatible services. fs = S3FileSystem( bucket="benchmark", key="minioadmin", secret="minioadmin", endpoint_url="http://localhost:9000", region="us-east-1", ) Anonymous access is available with anon=True.

S3 reads support optional Rust-side cache strategies through cache_type: cache_type Behavior none Fetch each requested byte range directly. readahead Keep one lookahead window for sequential reads. block Cache fixed-size blocks with LRU eviction. all Fetch the whole object on first read. with fs.open( "large/table.parquet", "rb", cache_type="block", block_size=8 * 1024 * 1024, ) as f: header = f.read(4096) block_size defaults to 4 MiB, and the Rust max_blocks default is 32. The Python file wrapper does not forward max_blocks from open(), so callers cannot change it through that method. Without an explicit cache_type, S3 read mode eagerly loads the whole object into memory. Explicit readahead, block, and none select range-based reads.

Exclude it: auditwheel repair --exclude 'libfsspec.so*' dist/*.whl delvewheel repair --exclude fsspec.dll dist/*.whl On macOS, delocate resolves every dependency before it applies --exclude, and your extension’s @rpath only finds libfsspec inside an environment where fsspec_rs is installed. Put the library from an fsspec-rs wheel on DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH while repairing: python -m pip download --no-deps --only-binary=:all: --dest fsspec-rs-wheel 'fsspec-rs>=0.2.1,<0.3' python -m zipfile -e fsspec-rs-wheel/fsspec_rs-*.whl fsspec-rs-wheel DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=fsspec-rs-wheel/fsspec_rs/lib delocate-wheel --exclude libfsspec dist/*.whl Require fsspec-rs at run time, at least the version you built against: [project] dependencies = ["fsspec-rs>=0.2"] To fail early on a mismatched library, compare fsspec_abi_version() with FSSPEC_ABI_VERSION (fsspec_sys::abi_version() in Rust) when your library loads.

Backend crates export one, and the application registers it once at startup: use std::sync::Arc; use fsspec_rs::{register_filesystem, FsOptions, LocalFs, SharedFileSystem}; register_filesystem("scratch", |_path: &str, _options: &FsOptions| { Ok(Arc::new(LocalFs::with_auto_mkdir(true)) as SharedFileSystem) }); To keep registrations out of the process-wide registry, build a FilesystemRegistry and call register and url_to_fs on it. In a process that loads the shared libfsspec (every wheel built from this repository, and any extension linked against it), fsspec_sys::use_shared_registry() routes register_filesystem and url_to_fs through that library, so a protocol registered by one extension is visible to every other crate in the process. Call it once before registering anything

s: Call a Python fsspec backend from Rust
x: Use the bridge crate in a Python extension or embedded-Python application. It requires Python and fsspec at runtime: [dependencies] fsspec_rs = "0.1.5" fsspec_rs_bridge = "0.1.5" Resolve a URL and call the filesystem trait: use fsspec_rs::FileSystem; use fsspec_rs_bridge::{url_to_fs, StorageOptions}; let (fs, _) = url_to_fs("memory://", &StorageOptions::new())?; fs.pipe_file("/example.txt", b"hello from Python fsspec")?; assert_eq!(fs.cat_file("/example.txt", None, None)?, b"hello from Python fsspec"); # Ok::<(), fsspec_rs::FsError>(()) For chained URLs, pass options in nested maps keyed by protocol: use fsspec_rs_bridge::{url_to_fs, StorageOptions}; let mut memory = StorageOptions::new(); memory.insert("skip_instance_cache".to_string(), true.into()); let mut options = StorageOptions::new(); options.insert("memory".to_string(), memory.into()); let (fs, path) = url_to_fs("simplecache::memory://bucket/data.csv", &options)?; # Ok::<(), fsspec_rs::FsError>(()) Within this repository’s workspace, use path dependencies ./rust and ./rust/bridge instead of registry versions. See Rust traits for backend primitives and bridge value types.

LocalFs and S3Fs implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. Backends must implement seven primitive methods and protocol: use fsspec_rs::{FileInfo, FileSystem, FsFile, FsResult, OpenMode, OpenOptions}; struct MyFs; impl FileSystem for MyFs { fn protocol(&self) -> &[&str] { &["myfs"] } fn ls(&self, path: &str, detail: bool) -> FsResult<Vec<FileInfo>> { todo!() } fn rm_file(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn cp_file(&self, src: &str, dst: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn open( &self, path: &str, mode: OpenMode, opts: Option<OpenOptions>, ) -> FsResult<Box<dyn FsFile>> { todo!() } fn info(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<FileInfo> { todo!() } fn mkdir(&self, path: &str, create_parents: bool) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn rmdir(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } } root_marker() defaults to "" and sep() defaults to "/". Backends can override them for local or platform-specific behavior. strip_protocol() and unstrip_protocol() also have defaults and can be overridden when a backend needs bucket-aware or authority-aware paths. The default methods built on those primitives include: Path helpers: strip_protocol, unstrip_protocol, parent Metadata checks: exists

FileSystem::read(path, ReadOptions) returns ReadResult { data, validator }. FileSystem::write(path, data, WriteOptions) returns WriteResult { validator } after committing the write. A validator, when available, describes the object read or committed by that operation. Obtain it from the result and pass it back unchanged; it contains an opaque scope and value, not a general content hash. Both options structs accept condition: Option<Condition>: Condition Read Write None Read current bytes. Replace or create. Match(validator) Read only the matching object. Replace only the matching object. Missing Invalid argument. Create only if absent. use fsspec_rs::{Condition, FileSystem, OperationError, ReadOptions, WriteOptions}; fn replace(fs: &dyn FileSystem, path: &str, data: &[u8]) -> Result<(), OperationError> { let current = fs.read(path, ReadOptions::default())?; let validator = current.validator.ok_or_else(|| { fsspec_rs::FsError::NotSupported("backend returned no validator".into()) })?; fs.write(path, data, WriteOptions { condition: Some(Condition::Match(validator)), })?; Ok(()) } ReadOptions.start and .end follow cat_file slicing semantics: negative offsets count from the end, bounds

FileSystem::read_ranges(path, &[ByteRange], RangeReadOptions) returns a RangeReadResult containing data: Vec<Vec<u8>> in input order and an optional shared validator. Each ByteRange { start, end } uses the same signed, optional bounds as read: ends are exclusive, negative offsets count from the end, bounds are clamped, and reversed ranges are empty. Duplicates and overlapping ranges each receive their own output buffer. RangeReadOptions accepts: Field Default Meaning condition None Optional Match(validator); Missing is invalid. max_gap 65,536 bytes Largest gap eligible for coalescing. Zero still merges adjacent or overlapping ranges. max_request_size 8,388,608 bytes Maximum data span per request; larger input ranges are split. Must be positive. max_concurrency 8 Maximum concurrent requests within this call. Must be positive. S3 reads metadata once, then pins data requests to its validator, including requests made without a caller-supplied Match. It rejects changed validators, response bounds or response lengths instead of returning partial results. All range-read calls and S3 instances using the same canonical endpoint share an additional cap of eight active requests, including met

AsyncFileSystem is the experimental async version of FileSystem. Its primitive methods return futures, and its default helpers are async fns. LocalFs and S3Fs implement only the synchronous FileSystem trait. AsyncFileSystem::open currently returns a blocking FsFile; awaiting open does not make subsequent reads asynchronous. The async I/O contract provides operation futures and managed/foreign callback dispatch in fsspec_rs::async_io, plus Rust futures over the shared library in fsspec_sys::async_io. Async file handles and shared byte budgets remain proposed. The default async implementation avoids recursive async futures in walk() by using an explicit stack. Method semantics otherwise match FileSystem.

FileSystem::open() returns a file implementing FsFile, which requires Read + Write + Seek + Send. commit() and discard() default to no-ops and are available for buffered writes or future transaction support. S3 writes require explicit commit(). Dropping an unfinished S3 writer discards its buffer and attempts to abort any multipart upload. This includes exclusive and append handles; Drop never publishes S3 content. Foreign handles reached through the C ABI also discard on Drop. Direct local append writes remain immediate, and generic BufferedFile retains its configured autocommit behavior.

FileInfo is the common metadata value. It stores: name: full path or backend path size: bytes, usually 0 for directories file_type: FileType::File, FileType::Directory, or FileType::Other created and modified: optional SystemTime values extra: backend-specific string metadata such as S3 ETags Convenience constructors are available: let file = FileInfo::file("/tmp/data.bin", 1024); let dir = FileInfo::directory("/tmp"); OpenMode::from_str_mode() accepts rb, wb, ab, xb, and the equivalent single-letter forms. OpenOptions::default() uses a 4 MiB block size, autocommit = true, no explicit cache strategy, and max_blocks = 32.

LocalFs uses std::fs and implements FileSystem. LocalFs::new() starts with auto_mkdir = false. LocalFs::with_auto_mkdir(true) creates missing parent directories during write, append, exclusive-create, and copy operations.

S3Fs wraps object_store::aws::AmazonS3 and runs its async calls through an embedded Tokio runtime to implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. S3Fs and the registry’s s3 protocol come from the s3 feature, which is on by default. With default-features = false the crate does not depend on object_store or Tokio and builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown: [dependencies] fsspec_rs = { version = "0.2", default-features = false } S3Config supports: bucket region endpoint_url access_key_id secret_access_key session_token anon virtual_hosted_style_request Plain HTTP is allowed automatically when endpoint_url starts with http://, which is useful for MinIO and LocalStack. Region precedence is explicit region, AWS_REGION, then AWS_DEFAULT_REGION; without any value the backend uses us-east-1. When no explicit credential field is supplied, static credentials come from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and optional AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. Key and secret are required together. Explicit credentials never inherit an environment token. Anonymous access ignores credential fields. Without static credentials, the existing instance-metadata provider remains available. Profiles, SSO and credential_process

Arc<S3Fs>::objects() returns a cloneable S3ObjectReader sharing the client’s credentials, runtime and range concurrency limit. head(key) returns native metadata as FileInfo, with FileType::File, modification time, and optional etag/version extras. It never infers directories. read_ranges(key, ranges) returns ordered bytes with a validator, using the existing S3 coalescing defaults. Both methods return OperationError. Keys are literal canonical bucket-relative paths, without URL or bucket stripping or the filesystem’s extra key escaping. Ranges require both signed 64-bit bounds, 0 <= start < end, and a start before EOF. Oversized ends are clipped; empty input performs no I/O. Ranged reads require an ETag and fail if the object changes. The reader keeps its client alive after the original filesystem handle is dropped. S3Fs::from_options(bucket, options) constructs the built-in backend using the same option validation as the S3 registry factory, without registry lookup or caching. The C ABI uses it to create paired filesystem and object-reader handles.

FilesystemRegistry maps URL protocols to FilesystemFactory implementations, the Rust counterpart of fsspec’s fsspec.specs entry points. Rust has no runtime plugin discovery, so a backend crate exports a factory and the application registers it. Any Fn(&str, &FsOptions) -> FsResult<SharedFileSystem> closure is a factory. url_to_fs(url, options) returns a SharedFileSystem and the path to pass to it. A URL without protocol:// is a local path. Options are a FsOptions (BTreeMap<String, String>). Chained URLs such as simplecache::s3://... are not supported. Filesystems are cached by protocol, options, and the factory’s instance_scope for the path, so equal calls share one instance. url_to_fs_uncached always builds a new one. Registering a protocol again replaces its factory and drops its cached instances. FilesystemRegistry::default() registers: Protocol Filesystem Options file, local LocalFs auto_mkdir memory MemoryFs, one per process none s3 S3Fs, one instance per bucket key, secret, token, endpoint_url, region, anon, virtual_hosted_style_request, connect_timeout, request_timeout, max_retries Registry and C options encode timeouts as finite positive seconds and max_retries as a nonnega

The optional object-store feature exports object_store_bridge::FileSystemStore and object_store_bridge::ObjectStoreFs. It can be enabled without S3: default-features = false, features = ["object-store"]. The default s3 feature also enables it. Neither adapter requires Python, registration, or a new trait. Backend implements Filesystem access Object access FileSystem only Native FileSystemStore object_store::ObjectStore only ObjectStoreFs Native Both Native Native Construction is explicit. No blanket trait implementations, automatic discovery, or adapter chaining are provided. A backend implementing both traits exposes its native interfaces directly over the same data. The compiling example is rust/examples/object_store_bridge.rs.

FileSystemStore::from_snapshot(Arc<dyn FileSystem + Send + Sync>, root) binds a read-only object view to an immutable filesystem namespace. The caller must keep names, metadata, and contents unchanged until the adapter and its streams are dropped. The constructor does not create a snapshot or prevent other handles from writing. Generic mutable-filesystem adaptation remains unsupported because FileSystem cannot atomically return both metadata and bytes. ObjectStore operation Behavior get_opts Read metadata and open a regular file within the immutable source; return lazy chunks. head avoids opening the body. Read conditions Evaluate ETag/time conditions against snapshot metadata. Version selection is unsupported. get_ranges Use the trait’s coalescing implementation over range reads. list Walk directories lazily and yield regular-file metadata under a segment-aware prefix. list_with_delimiter Return immediate objects and prefixes containing objects; empty filesystem directories disappear. Put, multipart, delete, copy, rename Unsupported; no mutation reaches the source. FileInfo.modified is required for object metadata. Missing timestamps and reported special files return NotSupported;

ObjectStoreFs::new(Arc<dyn ObjectStore>, prefix) binds relative filesystem paths to one object-store prefix. The adapter owns a shared client handle, not its credentials or a separate client. Root is ""; paths are parsed without percent encoding or decoding. URLs, absolute paths, backslashes and noncanonical paths are rejected. Listings also fail with NotSupported when returned names cannot be reopened through this mapping. No object:// protocol is registered automatically. FileSystem operation Behavior info Use native object metadata; infer directories from delimiter listings; root is a directory. ls Return objects and synthetic directories; reject object/prefix name collisions. open(Read, None) Return a seekable handle after metadata checks, without downloading the body. Handle reads Issue at most 64 KiB per request; use the opening version/ETag when available. Handle seeks Support absolute, relative and end-relative offsets; seeking past EOF is allowed. Mutations and explicit open options Unsupported. Metadata and listings are required, including for collision checks on open. Empty object-store prefixes have no persistent directory identity. fsspec_rs_bridge exports PyFsspecFs, url_to_fs, and StorageOptions. It is an rlib using PyO3 and Python fsspec at runtime, with no #[pyclass] exports. url_to_fs(url, options) returns a filesystem adapter and start path. PyFsspecFs::from_protocol(protocol, options) constructs an adapter by protocol. The adapter’s trait protocol is python; source_protocol() reports the wrapped protocol. The bridge initializes and attaches to the Python interpreter internally. PyFsspecFs implements FileSystem and delegates ls, info, open, cat_file, pipe_file, cp_file, rm_file, mkdir, rmdir, get_file, and put_file to Python. Common Python exceptions map to FsError categories. StorageOptions values support nulls, booleans, signed and unsigned integers, floats, strings, lists, and nested maps. Nested maps keyed by protocol configure chained URLs. The Rust guide includes dependency and invocation examples.

The caching layer is used by buffered reads. CacheType::from_str() accepts: Value Strategy none NoCache: every fetch goes to the backend. readahead or read_ahead ReadAheadCache: one lookahead window. block or blockcache BlockCache: fixed-size blocks with LRU eviction. all or bytes AllBytesCache: whole-file cache on first read. Each cache wraps a Fetcher, a FnMut(u64, u64) -> FsResult<Vec<u8>> that retrieves the half-open byte range [start, end) from the backend.

Except for typed object I/O, fallible filesystem methods return FsResult<T> = Result<T, FsError>. FsError represents filesystem errors with these variants: NotFound PermissionDenied AlreadyExists NotADirectory IsADirectory IoError InvalidArgument NotSupported Other The PyO3 layer maps those variants to Python exceptions such as FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, FileExistsError, NotADirectoryError, IsADirectoryError, ValueError, NotImplementedError, and OSError.
